name: Pontic Greek, Trapezountian variety as spoken in Etoloakarnania
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand sources agree (0 agree, 3 refine), none contradicts
catalog_citation: Armostis, Spyros, Louiza Voniati, Konstantinos Drosos & Dionysios Tafiadis. 2022. Trapezountian Pontic Greek in Etoloakarnania (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 52(2): 328-340. doi:10.1017/S0025100320000201
catalog_quote: As is the case with all Modern Greek varieties, words in Etoloakarnania Trapezountian Pontic Greek bear lexical stress, with the exception of clitics and some functional words. Stress is manifested as increased duration, higher intensity and changes in F0. Stress is contrastive, e.g. [kaˈla] καλά 'well' vs. [ˈkala] κάλλα 'better'. Most Modern Greek varieties restrict stress on one of the last three syllables of the word. Pontic Greek allows stress to fall beyond the third syllable from the end either due to inflectional endings or because of clitics that get attached on the stem, e.g. [ekaˈlat͡ʃevanemaˌsen] εκαλάτσ̆ευανεμασεν 'they were talking to us', [ˈestilanemaˌsen] έστειλανεμασεν 'they sent us', [ˈiðaˌnatune] είδαν'ατουνε 'they saw him'. In these cases there is a secondary stress on the first or third syllable from the end (see Kontosopoulos 2008: 15).

new_statements.quote: La langue est à accent libre (cf. P. Garde, 1968), comme du reste l'ensemble des dialectes grecs. Dans certains cas, la place de l'accent est pertinente. [...] Ce cas très régulier mis à part, la place de l'accent n'est pas prédictible au niveau phonologique, à ceci près qu'elle obéit à une règle de limitation : l'accent ne peut remonter au-delà de la septième syllabe comptée à partir de la fin du mot phonologique. Les enclitiques sont pris en compte dans cette limitation. [p. 48, §6] [...] l'accent pontique est certainement un des éléments les plus originaux de la langue au sein de l'ensemble grec puisqu'il n'applique pas la règle de limitation aux trois syllabes, à partir de la fin du mot [p. 49]
new_statements.translation: The language has free accent (cf. P. Garde 1968), as indeed do all the Greek dialects. In certain cases the place of the accent is distinctive. [...] Apart from this very regular case [the vocative retraction], the place of the accent is not predictable at the phonological level, except that it obeys a limitation rule: the accent cannot move back beyond the seventh syllable counted from the end of the phonological word. Enclitics are counted in this limitation. [p. 48] [...] the Pontic accent is certainly one of the most original elements of the language within the Greek group, since it does not apply the three-syllable limitation rule counted from the end of the word [p. 49]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has pont1253 with an empty rule field and no existing statements, so Drettas supplies the placement statement: free/lexical accent with a seven-syllable window and no three-syllable restriction. This is compatible with the Kooij & Revithiadou 2001 findings recorded in from the earlier reading ('Stress can occur on any syllable of the word'; 'Pontic lacks the three-syllable-window restriction'); Drettas adds the explicit seven-syllable limit including enclitics, the vocative and past-tense retractions, and the fixed-across-paradigm verbal accent. It does not state a default (initial) stress for accentless morphemes as K&R do; that point is neither confirmed nor contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is free and lexically fixed: minimal pairs exist ('poli 'city' vs po'li 'many'; 'pino 'I drink' vs pi'no 'I am hungry'; 'jeron 'old man' vs je'ron 'healthy'), and its position is not phonologically predictable. The only constraint is a window: the accent may lie no further left than the seventh syllable from the end of the phonological word, enclitics included (e.g. eka'latfevan.emasene 'they were talking to us'); the fourth syllable from the end (pre-antepenult) is the commonest extreme position, fifth to seventh are possible, mostly in verbs with enclitic objects. The Modern Greek three-syllable window does not apply. Morphological uses of accent shift: vocative singular retracts the accent up to three or four syllables (pa'tera(s) > 'patera; popa'dia > 'popadia; ko'ritsopon > 'koritsopon); in some verbs the past (augmented) forms retract the accent one syllable toward the word start ('leyne 'they say' / 'eleyan 'they said'), and otherwise the accent stays fixed across the whole verb paradigm (§289).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress rule is stated. p. 49 notes only that when other Greek speakers hear Pontic, elements outside the Greek accent grid 'become inaudible or are perceived as bearing a secondary accent'. §778 (localizers chapter) says the focus particle /-ki/ attached to the verb phrase 'porte le plus souvent un accent secondaire qui se réalise comme une chute tonale' (usually carries a secondary accent realized as a pitch fall). p. 46 (§3) describes a tonal rise ('montée tonale') between the future particle /tha-/ and the tonic syllable when combined with the negation /khi-/.
new_statements.exceptions: Vocative-singular accent retraction up to 3-4 syllables (p. 48); past-tense (imperfect/aorist) retraction of the accent by one syllable in some verb classes, no shift in others, e.g. 'pero / e'perna (§289, §292); an extra final syllable may be added in phrase-final position without moving the accent, giving accent on the fifth syllable from the end (e'fiumnestine, p. 49); enclitics (object pronouns, possessives, particle /-pa/, /kja/) count toward the seven-syllable limit; clitics (article, prepositions, verbal particles, negation) are stressless, and words like 'to be' and interrogatives can lose their accent and cliticize (pp. 45-47). Footnote 2 p. 49: Cypriot allows accent up to the fourth syllable from the end.
new_statements.identity_note: Drettas describes the Pontic of refugees settled in the village 'Xr.' (Almopia, Aridaia district, Greek Macedonia), whose families come overwhelmingly from Chaldia (Xaldhia): the villages Xukli, Gharenti, Atra, Xalkanton, Xuture and the town of Gümüshane (pp. 26-37, 'Composition du groupe pontique'); he states that the normative core of the refugees' common Pontic 'est fondé essentiellement sur la variété de la Xaldhia' (p. 25). This is the Chaldia variety, not the Trapezountian (Trebizond) variety as spoken in Etoloakarnania that the catalog name refers to. Drettas treats the accent facts (free accent, no three-syllable rule) as characteristic of Pontic in general ('caractéristique dialectale', §289), so the statement is used as applying to the language pont1253, but the sub-variety difference should be kept in the record.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is present verbatim at the stated place (p. 337, 'Stress') in the held Armostis et al. 2022 PDF text. (2) The source is a 2022 JIPA Illustration for exactly this sub-variety, by phoneticians with native consultants; a second held source (Schreiber 2024, pp. 56-58) and the newly downloaded dedicated accent study (Kooij & Revithiadou 2001, pp. 88-91) independently state lexical/phonemic stress with no three-syllable window, so the lexical / non-window coding is secure. (3) Kooij & Revithiadou refine rather than contradict: accentless words get default initial stress, there is no weight sensitivity, and secondary stress is doubtful -- the last point bears only on our the secondary-stress rule, which repeats Armostis et al.'s second-hand pointer to Kontosopoulos 2008: 15. sources.note: The one dedicated theoretical study of Pontic accentuation; adds what the JIPA paragraph lacks: default-initial stress for accentless words, root/head accent competition, no weight sensitivity, and doubt about secondary stress (our the secondary-stress rule asserts secondary stress on Kontosopoulos 2008's authority). downloaded now.
